name: 5S
definition: Methodology for workplace organization aimed at improving efficiency, reducing waste, and creating a structured, clean, and standardized work environment. It is often used as a foundational Lean tool to engage people and stabilize continuous improvement practices.
when_to_use: disorganized or cluttered workplace
difficulty finding tools, materials, or information
inefficient or inconsistent workstations
early stage of Lean transformation
need to engage employees in improvement initiatives
signals: tools or materials not in fixed locations
lack of standardization in workspace usage
implementation: Seiri: separate necessary from unnecessary items
Seiton: organize and assign a fixed place for necessary items
Seiso: clean workplace and equipment
Seiketsu: standardize the first three steps
Shitsuke: sustain discipline and continuous adherence
ensure system is designed for user needs, not just visual order
kpis: number of missing or misplaced items

name: Analisi di Pareto
definition: Method based on the Pareto Principle (80/20 rule) used to identify the small number of causes responsible for the majority of problems or outcomes. It helps prioritize efforts by focusing on the most impactful factors.
when_to_use: too many problems or defects with unclear priority
need to identify main drivers of inefficiency
limited resources and need for prioritization
high variability in causes of issues
decision making based on impact rather than volume
signals: many different types of recurring problems
resources spread across too many issues
lack of clarity on root causes
implementation: collect data on problems or occurrences
categorize causes or types of issues
quantify frequency or impact of each category
rank causes from highest to lowest impact
focus improvement efforts on top 20% of causes generating 80% of the impact
review results after intervention
kpis: percentage of problems coming from top causes
reduction in total defects or issues

name: Andon
definition: Visual management system used to signal the operational status of a machine, process, or work center in real time. It provides immediate visibility of normal operation, warnings, or critical issues using simple visual signals (typically colors).
when_to_use: need for real-time visibility of process status
frequent machine or process interruptions
need for immediate problem escalation
environments requiring fast response to issues
lack of transparency in operational status
signals: lack of real-time awareness of problems
delayed response to machine or process failures
implementation: define status indicators (green, yellow, red)
assign meaning to each signal (normal, warning, critical)
install visual signal system (lights, boards, digital displays)
enable operators to trigger alerts immediately
ensure escalation process is defined and fast

name: Asaichi
definition: Structured daily Lean meeting (often called Lean meeting) designed to align teams quickly and effectively at the Gemba. It ensures fast communication, visual management of KPIs, and operational alignment through short, standardized meetings focused on real operational data.
when_to_use: need for daily alignment between teams
inefficient or long meetings
lack of visibility on KPIs and operational status
frequent communication via email or fragmented updates
need to improve coordination in production or office workflows
signals: meetings are too long or unstructured
decisions delayed due to lack of shared information
implementation: schedule daily 15-minute meeting
conduct meeting at Gemba (real workplace)
use visual boards with real-time KPIs
standardize agenda and topics
define clear roles and speaking order
ensure participants arrive prepared
focus only on operational data and blockers

name: Diagramma di Ishikawa
definition: Root cause analysis tool used to systematically identify all possible causes of a specific problem. Also known as Cause-Effect Diagram or Fishbone Diagram, it helps structure problem-solving by categorizing causes and identifying the most impactful root drivers.
when_to_use: recurring or complex problems with unknown root causes
need to structure brainstorming around a specific issue
high-impact problem identified via prioritization (e.g. Pareto analysis)
need to involve team in structured problem solving
quality issues or operational inefficiencies without clear cause
signals: problem persists despite multiple attempts to fix it
lack of clarity on root cause
teams working on symptoms instead of causes
implementation: define the problem clearly and specifically
optionally prioritize problem using Pareto analysis
individually brainstorm possible causes
group causes into 4M categories: Manpower, Methods, Materials, Machines
optionally add Environment category
visualize causes in fishbone structure
conduct team review to validate most impactful causes
select root causes and define action plan

name: Finestra Kaizen
definition: Kaizen-based diagnostic tool used to analyze problems by comparing them against the existence and knowledge of operational standards. It shifts focus from blaming individuals to evaluating whether standards exist and are properly understood and applied.
when_to_use: recurring problems involving human behavior or errors
unclear responsibility between process and people
lack of adherence to operational standards
need to evaluate effectiveness of standardization
training or execution issues in teams
signals: tendency to blame individuals for process failures
lack of clarity on whether a standard exists
frequent mistakes despite procedures being defined
implementation: define the problem clearly
ask if a standard exists (Yes/No)
ask if the standard is known by operators (Yes/No)
map the situation into one of four quadrants
identify appropriate action based on quadrant
if standard exists but is unknown: train and communicate
if no standard exists: create and formalize one
if standard exists and is known but not followed: investigate enforcement or usability
if no standard and unknown: design process from scratch

name: Gemba
definition: Lean principle meaning 'the real place where value is created'. It refers to going to the actual workplace (factory, office, or operational environment) to observe processes directly, understand real problems, and make decisions based on facts rather than assumptions.
when_to_use: when a problem or anomaly occurs in a process
when decisions are being made without direct observation of operations
when root causes are unclear or based on assumptions
when improving operational efficiency or quality
when managers need better understanding of real work conditions
signals: decisions made without direct process observation
lack of visibility of actual operational conditions
reliance on reports instead of real data from the field
implementation: go to the actual workplace immediately when a problem occurs
observe the process directly (do not rely only on reports)
check Gembutsu (physical objects such as machines, tools, defects)
apply quick temporary countermeasures if needed
investigate root cause after stabilizing the situation
standardize the solution using SDCA (Standardize-Do-Check-Act)
ensure continuous presence of managers in operational areas
kpis: number of issues solved at root cause

name: Hansei
definition: Structured self-reflection practice used in Lean and Kaizen culture to learn from both successes and failures. It focuses on analyzing experiences objectively to improve future performance, without blame or self-judgment.
when_to_use: after completing a project or task
after a problem has been solved
when performance needs to be improved
after successful or unsuccessful outcomes
to institutionalize learning from experience

lack of feedback loops in processes

describe what actually happened
identify what went wrong and why
identify what went well and should be standardized
extract lessons learned
translate insights into actionable improvements
avoid blame or personal judgment
document reflections for future reference

name: 5 Why
definition: Iterative questioning technique used to identify the root cause of a problem by repeatedly asking 'Why?' until the underlying cause is discovered. It is often used in combination with other tools such as Ishikawa Diagram to deepen problem analysis.
when_to_use: need to identify root cause of a specific problem
recurring issues with unknown origin
after initial problem categorization (e.g. Ishikawa)
when superficial fixes are not effective
when team needs structured problem investigation
signals: problem keeps repeating despite corrective actions
symptoms are treated but issue persists
lack of deep understanding of cause-effect relationship
implementation: define the problem clearly
ask 'Why did this happen?'
repeat the question at least 5 times or until root cause is identified
validate each answer with facts (preferably via Gemba)
avoid jumping to solutions too early
link findings with Ishikawa categories if needed
identify final root cause
define corrective action based on root cause
kpis: number of problems solved at root cause level
percentage of problems resolved without recurrence

name: Ishikawa Diagram
definition: Structured root cause analysis tool (also called Fishbone or Cause-Effect Diagram) used to identify and organize all possible causes of a problem. kpis: number of validated root cause hypotheses

name: Kaikaku
definition: Lean concept referring to radical, breakthrough change in processes, systems, technology, or organizational structure. Unlike Kaizen (continuous incremental improvement), Kaikaku focuses on disruptive improvements that significantly change performance or operating models.

name: Kaizen
definition: Kaizen is the Lean philosophy of continuous improvement through small, incremental changes involving all employees. It focuses on improving processes daily by eliminating waste and engaging people directly involved in value creation.

name: Kanban
definition: Kanban is a visual pull-based workflow management system used in Lean production to control inventory and production flow. It ensures that work is triggered by actual demand (pull system) rather than forecast, enabling Just-In-Time production and reducing overproduction.

excess inventory or overproduction issues
lack of synchronization between processes
need for Just-In-Time production
unpredictable or fluctuating demand
need to reduce lead time and improve flow efficiency

poor coordination between upstream and downstream processes

attach Kanban card (visual signal) to each container

define pull rules between downstream and upstream processes
use consumption as trigger for production replenishment
track lead time and consumption rates
continuously adjust Kanban limits based on demand
ensure no production without Kanban signal

nothing is produced without a Kanban signal
flow is controlled visually and physically
focus on Just-In-Time (JIT) delivery
kpis: percentage of work triggered by pull signals

name: Just-In-Time (JIT)
definition: Just-In-Time is a Lean production philosophy that ensures materials and products are delivered exactly when needed, in the required quantity and quality. It aims to eliminate waste by producing only what is needed, when it is needed, and where it is needed.

name: Lead Time
definition: Lead Time is the total time required for a process to be completed, from the moment a request or order is initiated to the final delivery to the customer. In Lean thinking, it represents the total time of flow across the entire value stream.

name: Lean Manufacturing
definition: Lean Manufacturing is a production philosophy derived from the Toyota Production System focused on maximizing customer value while minimizing waste (Muda). It emphasizes continuous improvement, flow efficiency, and respect for people. It integrates tools and methodologies to create a 'lean' (streamlined) system that delivers value with minimal resources.

definition: Mizusumashi is a Lean logistics role responsible for material supply within production areas, typically operating through Milk Run systems. It ensures timely and standardized delivery of materials to production lines using predefined routes and schedules, often supported by logistic trains (tugger trains).

name: Muda
definition: Muda refers to any activity that does not add value from the customer's perspective. It is one of the three categories of waste in Lean thinking (Mura, Muri, Muda). Muda includes all inefficiencies within processes that consume resources without creating value, and it is considered the most critical type of waste because it often generates Mura (unevenness) and Muri (overburden).
when_to_use: need to improve process efficiency
high operational costs without value creation

process mapping and optimization (Value Stream Mapping)

Excess stored materials or products that tie up capital, hide problems, and increase risk of damage or obsolescence.
Unnecessary movement of people that does not add value and may cause inefficiency or ergonomic issues.
Idle time when people or processes are waiting, causing loss of productivity and flow interruption.
Producing more than customer demand, considered the most critical waste as it generates other wastes.
Non-conforming products or errors requiring rework, scrap, or causing customer dissatisfaction.
Unnecessary processing steps that do not add value and often result from poor process design or lack of synchronization.

name: Mura

name: Muri
definition: Muri refers to overburden or excessive strain placed on people, machines, or processes. name: OEE
definition: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) is a key manufacturing KPI that measures the true efficiency of production equipment by combining Availability, Performance, and Quality into a single metric. It identifies how effectively a manufacturing operation is utilized compared to its full potential.

components.definition: Measures the percentage of planned production time that the equipment is actually operational.

components.name: Performance

name: One Piece Flow
definition: One Piece Flow is a Lean production method where products move through each process step one unit at a time, instead of in batches. It minimizes work-in-progress (WIP), reduces waiting times, and significantly shortens lead time by ensuring continuous flow of single items through the production system.

name: PDCA (Deming Cycle)
definition: PDCA is a structured continuous improvement cycle developed by William Edwards Deming. It is used to solve problems, test improvements, and standardize successful changes through an iterative four-step process: Plan, Do, Check, Act.

phases.name: Plan
phases.description: Identify and analyze the problem or opportunity, define objectives, and develop hypotheses or potential solutions to test.

phases.name: Do
phases.description: Implement the proposed solution on a small scale and collect data to observe its effects.

phases.name: Check
phases.description: Evaluate the results, compare them against expectations, and determine the effectiveness of the solution.

phases.name: Act
phases.description: If successful, standardize the solution and integrate it into regular operations. If not, refine and restart the cycle.

name: Poka-Yoke
definition: Poka-Yoke is a Lean technique designed to prevent errors before they occur or to immediately detect them when they happen. It is a 'mistake-proofing' system aimed at achieving zero defects by eliminating human errors in critical process steps.

name: Shu-Ha-Ri
definition: Shu-Ha-Ri is a Japanese learning model used in Lean Thinking and continuous improvement cultures. It describes the progression of mastery through three stages: learning fundamentals, breaking rules with understanding, and achieving creative mastery.
origin: Japanese martial arts / Toyota Learning Culture

stages.description: The learner strictly follows standard work and learns fundamentals through repetition. The Sensei provides guidance and responsibility, protecting the learner from failure.
The learner begins to understand the principles behind the rules and can adapt them with limited supervision. Creativity starts to emerge while respecting standards.
The learner fully internalizes the principles and can innovate freely. Standards become part of intuition, enabling mastery and continuous innovation.

name: SMART Goals
definition: SMART is a structured framework used to define clear, actionable, and measurable objectives in project management and continuous improvement contexts. It ensures goals are well-defined, trackable, and achievable within a given timeframe.
origin: Project Management methodology (widely adopted in Lean, Agile, and business strategy)
when_to_use: project planning

criteria.name: Specific
criteria.description: The goal must be clear and unambiguous, leaving no room for interpretation.

criteria.name: Measurable
criteria.description: The goal must include measurable indicators (KPIs) to track progress and success.

criteria.name: Achievable
criteria.description: The goal must be realistic and attainable with available resources and constraints.

criteria.name: Relevant
criteria.description: The goal must be meaningful, aligned with business objectives and valuable for stakeholders.

criteria.name: Time-bound
criteria.description: The goal must have a defined deadline or time horizon.

name: SMED

name: Spaghetti Chart

benefits: increased team involvement in improvement activities
signals: materials repeatedly moved between distant points
frequent delays due to searching or fetching items
high physical workload without value-added activity
key_principles: movement that does not add value is waste

name: Standard Work
definition: Standard Work is a Lean methodology used to define, document, and stabilize the best known way to perform a process. Its goal is to reduce variability, ensure repeatability, and create a stable foundation for continuous improvement.
meaning: The best known way to perform a task, until a better method is discovered
when_to_use: when processes show high variability
when quality is inconsistent
when training new employees
to stabilize improvements from Kaizen activities
in repetitive production or service processes
when scaling operations across teams
definition_principle: Standard Work defines the best known method to perform a task, ensuring stability and enabling continuous improvement.

steps.description: Study how the work is actually performed in real conditions.
Define the most efficient, safe, and repeatable way to execute the process.
Record sequence, timing, and work-in-process clearly and visually.
Engage operators in understanding and applying the standard.
Ensure consistent application of the standard across shifts and operators.
Use Kaizen to refine the standard and update it when better methods are found.

key_principles: variation is the enemy of efficiency
important_quote: Improvement needs standardization, and standardization needs improvement
benefits: foundation for Kaizen and continuous improvement

name: Supermarket
definition: Il Supermarket è un’area di stoccaggio controllata utilizzata nei sistemi Lean e Pull, progettata per gestire materiali e componenti secondo logiche Kanban. È ispirato al funzionamento dei supermercati, dove il rifornimento è guidato dal consumo effettivo.
key_points: Area di prelievo per componenti gestiti in logica Pull/Kanban
Ogni materiale ha una posizione standardizzata e visibile
Le giacenze sono dimensionate tramite Kanban e numero di contenitori
Il rifornimento è attivato dal consumo reale (sistema Pull)
Garantisce logiche FIFO e controllo visuale delle scorte
benefits: Riduzione delle scorte e del WIP
Maggiore facilità di prelievo per gli operatori
Miglioramento del flusso logistico e della standardizzazione

name: Takt Time
definition: Il Takt Time è il tempo disponibile per produrre un’unità di prodotto in modo da soddisfare la domanda del cliente. Rappresenta il ritmo di produzione necessario per essere allineati alla richiesta del mercato.
key_points: Deriva dal tedesco 'Takt' che significa ritmo
È il ritmo di produzione imposto dalla domanda del cliente
Si calcola come tempo disponibile diviso domanda del cliente
Si esprime in unità tempo per pezzo (min/pezzo o sec/pezzo)
Agisce come un 'metronomo' per la produzione

formula.expression: Takt Time = Tempo disponibile / Domanda cliente

benefits: Allineamento della produzione alla domanda reale
Supporto all’implementazione di Just-In-Time e Pull
Maggiore visibilità del ritmo produttivo richiesto
risks_if_not_respected: Sovrapproduzione se il tempo ciclo è troppo basso
Incapacità di soddisfare il cliente se il tempo ciclo è troppo alto
Accumulo di scorte o ritardi nella consegna

name: Tempio TPS
definition: Il Tempio del Toyota Production System rappresenta la struttura concettuale del TPS, dove obiettivi, principi e fondamenta del sistema produttivo Toyota sono organizzati in forma di tempio.
key_points: Rappresenta visivamente la struttura del Toyota Production System
Il tetto simboleggia la soddisfazione del cliente
Gli obiettivi principali sono Quality, Cost e Delivery (QCD)
Le colonne portanti sono Just-In-Time e Jidoka
Le fondamenta sono Standard Work, Kaizen e Heijunka
benefits: Fornisce una visione sistemica del TPS
Aiuta a comprendere le relazioni tra strumenti Lean
Chiarisce il ruolo di qualità, flusso e stabilità
Supporta la formazione e la diffusione del Lean Thinking
Rende esplicito il legame tra stabilità e miglioramento continuo

name: TPM (Total Productive Maintenance)
definition: Il TPM (Total Productive Maintenance) è una metodologia del Lean Manufacturing che mira a massimizzare l’efficienza degli impianti attraverso il coinvolgimento di tutta l’organizzazione nella manutenzione e cura delle attrezzature.
key_points: Coinvolge tutta l’organizzazione: operatori, manutentori e management
Trasforma la manutenzione in una responsabilità condivisa
Mira al miglioramento dell’OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness)
Promuove manutenzione preventiva e migliorativa
Sviluppa autonomia negli operatori per piccoli interventi quotidiani
principles: Manutenzione autonoma da parte degli operatori
Prevenzione dei guasti prima che accadano
Miglioramento continuo delle condizioni degli impianti
Pulizia e standardizzazione delle attrezzature
Coinvolgimento totale dell’azienda
benefits: Maggiore sicurezza sul posto di lavoro
Riduzione dei costi di manutenzione correttiva

name: Value Stream Mapping (VSM)
definition: La Value Stream Mapping è una metodologia Lean utilizzata per mappare e analizzare il flusso del valore, includendo tutte le attività a valore aggiunto e non, necessarie per trasformare una materia prima in un prodotto finito o per erogare un servizio.
key_points: Mappa il flusso del valore dal cliente alla consegna del prodotto
Include sia attività a valore aggiunto che non a valore aggiunto
Analizza flussi di materiali e informazioni
Aiuta a identificare sprechi (Muda) lungo il processo
È rappresentata tramite simboli standard di processo, materiali e informazioni

formula.expression: Indice di flusso = Lead Time di produzione / Tempo di processo
formula.interpretation: Più l’indice è vicino a 1, più il flusso è efficiente

benefits: Identifica inefficienze e sprechi lungo il processo
Supporta la progettazione di processi più snelli
Migliora la comunicazione tra funzioni aziendali
Guida il miglioramento continuo dei processi
important_principle: Il miglioramento non deriva dagli strumenti in sé, ma dal cambiamento della mentalità e dal coinvolgimento delle persone

name: Visual Management
definition: Il Visual Management è un approccio del Lean Thinking che utilizza strumenti e segnali visivi per rendere immediatamente comprensibili informazioni, stati ed anomalie all’interno dei processi aziendali, facilitando il controllo e il miglioramento delle attività.
key_points: Basato su comunicazione visiva immediata e intuitiva
Riduce la necessità di comunicazione gerarchica tradizionale
Rende visibili stati, anomalie e sprechi
Supporta l’azione immediata grazie alle informazioni visive
Favorisce standardizzazione e miglioramento continuo

concept.visual_factory: Fabbrica in cui il controllo e il coordinamento avvengono tramite segnali visivi

benefits: Rende visibili le anomalie a tutti
Aumenta la comprensione degli standard operativi
Migliora la sicurezza e l’efficienza del lavoro

tool_details.visual_control_board: Sistema fisico con KPI e indicatori visivi per monitorare attività e performance
tool_details.footprint: Marcature a pavimento che indicano la posizione corretta degli oggetti
tool_details.shadow_board: Pannelli con sagome degli strumenti per facilitare ordine e controllo
tool_details.andon: Sistema di segnalazione visiva dello stato operativo

principle: Avere informazioni visibili è il modo più rapido per trasformare la comprensione in azione

name: WIP (Work In Process)
definition: Il WIP (Work In Process) rappresenta tutti i prodotti o elementi che si trovano in fase di lavorazione o in attesa di essere lavorati all’interno di un processo produttivo o operativo.
key_points: Include tutto ciò che è in lavorazione o in attesa di lavorazione
È un indicatore del livello di carico del sistema produttivo
Influenza direttamente il Lead Time
È presente sia in produzione che nei processi d’ufficio
Deve essere monitorato per evitare inefficienze

concepts.little_law: Il Lead Time è proporzionale al WIP e al tempo ciclo del processo

effects_of_high_wip: Accumulo di scorte e materiali in processo
benefits_of_reducing_wip: Maggiore qualità e controllo del processo
applications: Uffici (documenti in attesa, email non processate)
